references.excerpt: Lead time is the interval between defined earlier and later detection events. Lead-time bias occurs when that timing difference is mistaken for a better outcome. In a fictional course, detection at year 4 and death at year 6 gives two years from diagnosis. Moving detection to year 3 with death still at year 6 gives three recorded years without adding life. Similarly, labelling post-treatment recurrence at a blood signal before imaging confirmation can mechanically lengthen survival measured from recurrence. Align the endpoint, qualifying event and clock origin. Ten months of detection lead time is not ten added months of life. Earlier effective intervention could help, but its benefit needs separate evidence; correcting the clock alone does not solve selection, confounding or missing follow-up.

In ctDNA monitoring studies, measured lead time is the date of a defined later event minus the date of the first qualifying positive blood sample, and it is conditional: a median over people with both an earlier positive and a later recurrence leaves out recurrences with no earlier positive, and people who are positive but have not yet recurred are censored.

references.excerpt: An evidence card records population, stage, treatment context and selection; specimen, handling, assay version and quality criteria; the reference condition or care comparator and its limitations; outcome and measurement time; the analysis plan, all tuning and independent evaluation; failed samples, dropout and missing outcomes; and sample size, intervals and remaining uncertainty. A response endpoint is not recurrence or survival. A preclinical card names the actual model and tested claim; an observational clinical association retains possible confounding. Neither alone establishes that the proposed clinical action helps. A headline metric also needs the consequences of false positive and false negative calls attached to the action. Distinguish prespecified analyses from exploratory searches, keep their tuning history, and seek confirmation that does not reuse the search. State whether a treatment-study denominator includes everyone assigned, only those treated or only those evaluable.

A model evaluated at a second hospital may still address advanced treated disease rather than the proposed postoperative use. Discrimination asks whether outcomes are ranked usefully; calibration asks whether stated probabilities agree with observed frequencies in comparable groups. Good ranking can coexist with inflated risk estimates, and good prognostic probabilities do not establish benefit from a treatment printed beside them. There is no single performance cutoff that makes every decision appropriate. If unchanged Hospital A samples are rerun, request an evaluation set held out from every tuning choice, a locked method, target population and outcome, all failure denominators and uncertainty. Internal resampling and independent external evaluation answer different performance questions; neither name alone is a clinical-use verdict.
